P2: The PostHog capture `timestamp` is set to `new Date()` at delivery time inside the worker. Because the outbox intentionally retries delayed events for up to seven days, a queued or retried event (e.g. `support_glasses_connected`, `support_failure_observed`) is stamped with when it was finally delivered rather than when the transition actually happened — the observed time only survives as the `support_last_observed_at` property and is never surfaced as the event timestamp. This mis-dates events in PostHog timelines/segmentation, which runs counter to OS-1886's goal of historical, meaningful-transition events. Consider passing the original observed time through enqueue (a dedicated event-time field on the outbox row) and using it as the `timestamp` so retried deliveries stay correctly backdated.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Prevent frozen globals from retaining request state**

On Node versions that take this `DONT_CONTEXTIFY` branch, a bundle or render request that runs `Object.freeze(globalThis)` can now freeze the actual context global; the old contextified sandbox throws on that freeze. `runInVM` injects per-request `renderingRequest`, `sharedExecutionContext`, and `runOnOtherBundle` onto this same object and clears them in `finally` by assignment, so once the global is frozen the cleanup throws/fails and those request-specific values remain visible to later requests that reuse the pooled VM.

This looks correct: `vm.createContext(DONT_CONTEXTIFY)` returns the new context's real `globalThis` rather than contextifying the sandbox object, so `Object.assign` onto it is the right way to inject the source-map hooks / `supportModules` globals / `additionalContext`. `contextObject` isn't referenced again after this block, so there's no aliasing hazard between the two branches despite one reusing the same object identity as the context and the other not.

This is a functional/breaking change, not a docs fix — raising the gem's minimum Rails dependency from `>= 5.2` to `>= 7.1` will make `bundle install`/`bundle update` fail for any consumer currently on Rails 6.x or 7.0, even if their app doesn't use any Rails-7.1-specific API. The PR justifies this by "CI only tests Rails 7.1," but "only tested against X" isn't the same claim as "requires X" — plenty of the code (e.g. the `compact_blank` polyfill in `configuration.rb` explicitly written "to support Rails 5.2-6.0") suggests the gem currently works on older Rails.

Given the repo's own changelog convention (see the Ruby 3.3+ floor bump, `CHANGELOG.md` around the "Ruby 3.3+ is required for React on Rails v17" entry), a dependency-floor bump like this should:
- Get its own `CHANGELOG.md` entry under `Unreleased` (per `.claude/docs/changelog-guidelines.md`: "breaking changes" are explicitly in-scope, unlike pure doc fixes which are excluded)
- Probably ship as its own PR with a version-bump/migration note, not bundled silently into a "fix incorrect docs" PR

`add_extract_loader_to_server_config` matches `GET_LOADER_PATH_JS` as an exact byte string. If the app’s existing `getLoaderPath` helper differs (whitespace/newlines/CRLF, or a user edit), the fallback branch will insert a second `function getLoaderPath(...)` with the same name, creating duplicate function declarations in the generated config. This can be confusing at best and can change behavior depending on which declaration “wins” in the final file.

Consider detecting an existing `getLoaderPath` by regex and, when present but not byte-identical, inserting only `EXTRACT_LOADER_JS` after that existing function instead of injecting a new helper.

b_body: `resolveErrorPolicy` now forwards `error.message` for plain `Error`s when status is undefined. Since `error.message` can be arbitrarily long, this can bloat MCP responses and logs unexpectedly. The no-subcommand form of `shaka-perf servers` stops at an interactive menu after starting containers; it does not itself launch the app processes. The repository's bundled twin-server instructions explicitly distinguish `servers start-servers` as the command that runs Overmind and warn that the no-subcommand form requires a human. Consequently, an automated or copy/paste user following this snippet will be left without servers on ports 3020/3030, and the subsequent `compare` command will fail to connect. Show the separate `start-containers` and backgrounded `start-servers` commands, or explicitly document the required menu interaction.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
b_body: The inline comment implies `shaka-perf servers` always starts the app servers, but the twin-servers flow is typically build → start containers → interactive menu (then start servers). As written, readers may expect the command to fully boot both sides without further steps.

🟡 The awk in the completeness-lint's scan loop (check-allowlist-completeness.sh:60-81) tracks the enclosing function name (`fn`) incorrectly in two ways: it never resets `fn` when a function body ends, so a symbol hit on any line between two top-level functions gets misattributed to the *previous* function instead of being recognized as outside any function; and for a receiver method like `func (h *helper) pauseViaMethod(...)`, the name-extraction logic strips the token down to an empty string, which both drops that method's own symbol hits and can reset the misattribution state early. No test in the current tree triggers either path, so this is a latent robustness gap rather than a live false negative today.
